svg.aria-label: Diagram: AWS Organizations declarative policies are enforced in the service's control plane, which AWS describes as an important distinction from authorization policies such as service control policies and resource control policies. Authorization policies regulate access to APIs, while declarative policies are applied directly at the service level to enforce durable intent. A service control policy governs principals by controlling the maximum available access permissions of principals at an API level and does not govern service-linked roles. A resource control policy does the same for resources at an API level and also does not govern service-linked roles. A declarative policy enforces the desired configuration of an AWS service without using API actions, and it does govern service-linked roles. Because it asserts a value rather than enumerating denied calls, the configuration is always maintained for supported attributes when the service adds new features or APIs, and is maintained when new accounts are added to the organization, which inherit the policy automatically. The catch is that a declarative policy is a position held rather than a change applied: if it is detached, the attribute state rolls back to its previous state before the policy was attached, and while it is attached an account cannot modify the setting directly. The account status report shows the current status of all supported attributes for accounts in scope.
svg.title: An SCP decides whether the call is allowed; a declarative policy decides what the value is
svg.text: Three organization policies, and the difference is where they act.
“While authorization policies regulate access to APIs, declarative policies are applied directly at the service level.”
AUTHORIZATION POLICIES — at the API
SCP: “controlling the maximum available access
permissions of principals at an API level”
RCP: the same, for resources.
Governs service-linked roles? No · No
DECLARATIVE POLICY — in the control plane
“enforcing the desired configuration of an AWS
service without using API actions”
There is no principal to evaluate, so none to exempt.
Governs service-linked roles? Yes
An enumerated deny list needs maintaining as APIs appear. A declared value does not.
“Once attached, the configuration is always maintained when the service adds new features or APIs.”
“Accounts joining an organization will automatically inherit the declarative policy in the organization.”
Which is the answer to the per-account, per-Region drift problem in #102.
The catch: it is a position held, not a change applied
“If a declarative policy is detached, the attribute state will roll back to its previous state before the
declarative policy was attached.”
Detaching during an incident does not leave the estate at the declared baseline. It restores what was hidden.
While attached
“you can’t modify the setting directly within an
account” — the local switch is gone.
And you can read what is in force
“The account status report allows you to review the
current status of all attributes … in scope.”
Before you attach one, record what each account’s prior state was.
That is the state you return to on detach. Without it, removing a policy is an action whose per-account outcome
you cannot predict.
Fine, as long as nobody reads “compliant while the policy is attached” as “compliant”.
